output.title: Skin-irritation / adhesion tag cluster — check against known adhesive-lift characterization
output.summary: Telemetry for adhesion_flag and skin_temp_delta_c is essentially flat between the prior and current windows, and a firmware comparison (1.4.0 vs 1.4.2) shows no version-driven difference in adhesion_flag rate (ratio CI spans one). Support-feedback volume tagged skin-irritation/adhesion rose modestly (from {f_6} to {f_5} matched records) but the sample text is consistent with the already-documented, open high-motion/high-skin-temperature adhesive lift characterization (KI-AD-007) rather than a new failure mode. The knowledge base explicitly warns against closing such clusters as 'expected' and instead calls for lot-level escalation, so this cannot be waved away, but the current data does not show a new or worsening driver either.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The skin-irritation/adhesion feedback cluster tracks the pre-existing, open high-motion and elevated-skin-temperature adhesive lift characterization rather than a new firmware-, app-, or region-specific regression; device-level telemetry rates for adhesion_flag and skin_temp_delta_c did not rise materially between windows.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A new adhesive lot defect (similar in shape to the previously confirmed INC-2025-031 lot recall) is driving the current cluster.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Cross-tabulate the skin-irritation/adhesion feedback records by pouch lot code and device manufacture date; a concentration in one lot would indicate a hardware batch issue rather than the general characterization.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A specific firmware version change increased adhesion_flag rates.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Repeat the firmware version-pair comparison across all available firmware versions and windows; ci_excludes_one already returned false for 1.4.0 vs 1.4.2, weakening a firmware-driver story.

deterministic_findings.label: adhesion_flag rate ratio, firmware 1.4.0 vs 1.4.2, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Feedback record volume tagged skin-irritation and adhesion increased from prior to current window ({f_6} to {f_5} records), which is consistent with a live, ongoing cluster.

Sample feedback text describes lifting during high-intensity sessions with redness/heat under the patch, matching the documented mechanism for high motion intensity plus elevated skin-temperature delta.

counter_evidence.claim: adhesion_flag telemetry rate is nearly unchanged between prior ({f_2}) and current ({f_1}) windows, showing no material worsening at the device level.
skin_temp_delta_c telemetry rate actually declined slightly from prior ({f_4}) to current ({f_3}), which does not support an environmental-driver escalation.
Comparing adhesion_flag rate across firmware 1.4.0 vs 1.4.2 in the current window gives a ratio of {f_7} with a confidence interval that includes one, indicating no detectable firmware-driven effect.

recommended_actions.description: Escalate the current skin-irritation/adhesion feedback cluster to operations per playbook guidance rather than closing tickets as an accepted characteristic; request lot codes from the sampled tickets to check for a lot-specific concentration akin to the prior confirmed hardware recall.
Continue monitoring adhesion_flag and skin_temp_delta_c telemetry with a breakdown by cohort and region over the next window to detect any emerging divergence from the flat baseline observed here.
Do not issue any external communication or product change based on current evidence; telemetry does not show a new or worsening signal beyond the already-open known-issue characterization.

uncertainty: Feedback record counts are small-sample (see {f_5} and {f_6}) and were not tested for statistical significance against expected ticket-volume variance.
No lot-code or device-batch data was available through these tools, so the possibility of a new hardware lot defect (as in INC-2025-031) could not be ruled in or out.

The triage candidate's affected-user and prior-event counts do not obviously match the feedback-search record counts returned here ({f_5} current, {f_6} prior); the discrepancy in counting method was not reconciled within this investigation.
activity_level or motion_intensity breakdowns were not queried, so the specific high-motion/high-delta subgroup characterization was not directly re-verified against current-window data.

output.title: Rising claims-interpretation ticket cluster: readiness score read as clinical result
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the claims-interpretation ticket rise to on-screen misreading of readiness scores, not a device defect. A targeted check of adhesion_flag telemetry (current vs prior window, with regional breakdown) found no material rate increase and no regional concentration, which does not contradict the hypothesis but also does not rule out other sensor-accuracy pathways for the data-accuracy co-tagged tickets. The specific falsifying test is a telemetry-confirmed, ticket-aligned spike in a sensor-accuracy metric; that was not observed for adhesion_flag, so status is downgraded to UNCERTAIN pending checks of additional metrics and device-level linkage.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The rise in claims-interpretation tickets is associated with wearers reading the on-screen readiness score or label as a clinical verdict, mirroring the previously documented claims-misread pattern rather than any change in sensor accuracy or hardware behavior.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A genuine sensor- or scoring-level accuracy problem (e.g., adhesion or motion-sensing anomaly affecting readiness score computation) is producing scores wearers correctly perceive as inconsistent with their felt state, which then get logged as claims-interpretation tickets because they are also tagged data-accuracy, rather than the tickets reflecting pure misreading of a correctly computed score.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: If adhesion_flag (or another sensor-accuracy) telemetry rate shows a concurrent spike in the current window, concentrated in the same firmware/app/region cells generating the co-tagged tickets, that would support a genuine device-level driver and undercut the pure-misinterpretation account; a same-window adhesion_flag check across regions showed no such spike or regional concentration, which weakens this alternative.

deterministic_findings.label: claims-interpretation tickets also tagged data-accuracy, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Sample tickets from the current window explicitly describe treating the readiness score as a clinical or diagnostic result, matching the claims-misread symptom set.
The claims-interpretation ticket cluster spans multiple firmware and app versions across five regions, indicating no single firmware, app, or region concentration.

A closed historical incident with the same symptom shape was resolved as a confirmed communications incident, not a device incident, with copy review and a policy update as the remedy; scoring code was not rolled back.
The support playbook explicitly defines a claims-misread intake queue with the same symptoms, tagged claims-interpretation and often data-accuracy.

counter_evidence.claim: Most current-window claims-interpretation tickets are also tagged data-accuracy ({f_3} of {f_1}), leaving open the possibility that some fraction of reports involve genuine perceived inaccuracy rather than pure misinterpretation; this was not independently verified against telemetry in this investigation.

adhesion_flag telemetry rate in the current window was essentially unchanged from the prior window and showed no regional concentration, which is consistent with (but does not prove) the absence of a concurrent hardware/sensor-accuracy driver behind the ticket spike; this check only covered one candidate metric (adhesion_flag) and cannot rule out other accuracy pathways feeding the data-accuracy co-tag.

output.title: Overheating-tagged tickets trace to known Nordics cold-weather battery drain, not thermal safety issue
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the overheating tag cluster to mislabeled battery/app-UI reports tied to a known Nordics cold-weather drain characteristic, not a real thermal event. A falsifying test is to check whether any region or firmware subgroup shows a skin_temp_delta_c rate distinctly elevated above others, since a real localized heat effect would still show up in a subgroup breakdown even if diluted in the aggregate; a region/firmware breakdown run in this pass found no standout subgroup, which does not contradict the leading hypothesis, but the same breakdown is the correct ongoing falsifying check, and any future divergence in a subgroup would falsify the claim that there is no real thermal signal underlying the tag.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The overheating tag is a mislabeling of app-UI battery warning screens and subjective device-feels-warm-when-syncing reports that co-occur with a documented, accepted Nordics cold-weather battery drain characteristic; it is not evidence of an actual thermal or skin-temperature safety event.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A genuine, localized thermal effect exists in a firmware or regional subset of devices (e.g., a specific firmware build or Nordics-specific usage pattern), but is masked in the aggregate skin_temp_delta_c rate because it only affects a small fraction of devices while the rest behave normally.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Break down skin_temp_delta_c by region and by firmware_version for the current window: if any single region or firmware subgroup (e.g., nordics, or firmware 1.4.1) shows a skin_temp_delta_c rate meaningfully elevated above the other subgroups, that would falsify the claim that the overheating tag reflects no real thermal signal, since a genuine localized heat effect would be diluted rather than absent in the aggregate. A breakdown check performed in this pass shows region- and firmware-level rates clustered closely together with no standout subgroup, which is consistent with (but does not fully prove) the leading hypothesis; a future re-check with the same breakdown remains the falsifying test if a subgroup diverges.

supporting_evidence.claim: Overheating-tagged feedback co-occurs almost entirely with battery and app-ui tags, and sampled text describes battery drain in cold weather and an alarming sync screen rather than a hot device.
The pattern is essentially unchanged between the prior and current windows ({f_4} versus {f_3} matched records), consistent with a stable, known characteristic rather than a new emerging defect.
skin_temp_delta_c shows no meaningful increase current versus prior ({f_1} versus {f_2}), arguing against an actual heat event.
Nordics battery_drain_pct ({f_5}) is noticeably higher than UK ({f_6}), matching the magnitude the Known Issues Register records for the accepted regional cold-weather drain characteristic.
A prior incident describing Nordics winter drain tickets was closed as not-an-incident and encoded as a standing known issue with the same regional battery-drain shape.

counter_evidence.claim: The Known Issues Register explicitly forbids using skin_temp_delta_c as proof of cold or ambient temperature, and states its correlation with battery_drain_pct in Nordics is approximately zero, so the regional battery story and any thermal story must be evaluated independently rather than conflated.
